query: Starting from crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals, what single intervention could overcome the unresolved risk of structural or chemical instability during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the mechanism by which it would preserve stability, the predicted outcome relative to the same nanoparticles without the intervention, relevant temperature, time, and compositional boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a thermal-exposure experiment with measurements and failure criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

revised_generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a sub-nanometric high-entropy alloy cluster on a CeO2 nanorod support can overcome the risk of structural or chemical instability in near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals during operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime.
revised_generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals
revised_generation.intervention: Introduction of a sub-nanometric high-entropy alloy cluster on a CeO2 nanorod support
revised_generation.conditions: Operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime
revised_generation.mechanism: Hydrogen spillover effect and multielement mixing in quantum-sized regions
revised_generation.predicted_outcome: Higher activity during the reduction of NO by H2 and unique structural reversibility in response to repeated exposure to oxidative/reductive conditions
revised_generation.uncertainty: The stability of the sub-nanometric high-entropy alloy cluster under prolonged operation and the potential for scalability
revised_generation.falsification_experiment: Thermal-exposure experiment with measurements of catalytic activity and structural stability over time, using XANES spectra to monitor the oxidation state of the non-noble metals.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (NPs) have attracted significant attention as promising catalysts owing to the various unique synergistic effects originating from the nanometer-scale, near-equimolar mixing of five or more components to produce single-phase solid solutions. However, the study of sub-nanometer HEA clusters having sizes of less than 1 nm remains incomplete despite the possibility of novel functions related to borderline molecular states with discrete quantum energy levels. The present work demonstrates the synthesis of CeO2 nanorods (CeO2-NRs) on which sub-nanometer CoNiCuZnPd HEA clusters were formed with the aid of a pronounced hydrogen spillover effect on readily reducible CeO2 (110) facets. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications.
